questions.question: What is a foreground process in Linux?
questions.answer: A foreground process is one that runs in the terminal and occupies it completely until it finishes. While it is running, you cannot type or execute any other commands. You see its output in real time and can interact with it directly.

questions.question: What is a background process and how do you start one?
questions.answer: A background process runs independently of the terminal, allowing you to continue using the terminal for other tasks. You start one by adding an ampersand (&) at the end of the command. Linux immediately returns the Job ID and Process ID.

questions.question: What is a Linux repository?
questions.answer: A repository is a trusted, verified online server from which the package manager downloads software packages. It is analogous to a Play Store for Linux — centralized, safe, and verified. The package manager connects to repositories automatically when you run install commands.

questions.question: What is the difference between YUM, DNF, and APT?
questions.answer: They are all package managers but for different Linux distributions. YUM is used on Amazon Linux and CentOS. DNF is the newer replacement, used on Amazon Linux 2023 and RHEL 8+. APT is used on Ubuntu and Debian. They all install, update, and remove packages, just with slightly different syntax.

questions.question: What does the 'jobs' command do?
questions.answer: The 'jobs' command lists all background jobs running in the current terminal session. It shows the job number, status (Running, Stopped), and the command that was run. Note that it only shows jobs in your current shell session, not system-wide processes.

questions.question: What is a zombie process?
questions.answer: A zombie process is one that has finished executing but hasn't been removed from the process table because its parent process hasn't called wait() to collect the exit status. Zombies consume no CPU or memory — just a PID slot. Too many can exhaust the process table and prevent new processes from starting.

questions.question: What is SFTP and how does it differ from FTP?
questions.answer: SFTP is SSH File Transfer Protocol — a secure file transfer protocol that operates over an SSH connection on port 22. Unlike traditional FTP (port 21), SFTP encrypts both commands and data, making it safe to use over the internet. FTP transmits everything including passwords in plain text.

questions.question: What does 'ps aux' show?
questions.answer: ps aux shows a snapshot of all currently running processes on the system. The 'a' flag shows processes for all users, 'u' adds user/owner information, and 'x' includes daemon processes not attached to any terminal. Key columns include PID, %CPU, %MEM, STAT, and COMMAND.

questions.question: What do the STAT codes R, S, D, T, Z mean in ps aux?
questions.answer: R means Running (actively executing). S means Sleeping (idle, waiting for an event). D means Uninterruptible Sleep (waiting for hardware like disk I/O, cannot be killed). T means Stopped (paused, e.g., by Ctrl+Z). Z means Zombie (finished but not cleaned up by parent yet).

questions.question: What is the difference between 'systemctl start' and 'systemctl enable'?
questions.answer: 'systemctl start' launches the service immediately for the current session only. 'systemctl enable' configures the service to auto-start every time the system boots. On EC2, you almost always need both — start to run now, and enable so it survives reboots. Running enable alone does NOT start the service right now.

questions.question: You install a web application on EC2 and use systemctl start. After a reboot, the application is down and users are complaining. What happened and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: (Situation) Application crashed after EC2 reboot. (Task) Restore service and prevent recurrence. (Action) I identified that 'systemctl start' was used without 'systemctl enable'. While start runs the service now, enable is required to register it for auto-start at boot. I ran 'sudo systemctl enable appname' to fix this. (Result) The service now survives reboots automatically.

questions.question: You run a long data migration script and it will take 2 hours. You also need to monitor logs during this time. How do you set this up?
questions.answer: (Situation) 2-hour script, need terminal access simultaneously. (Task) Run both without blocking. (Action) I run the migration script in the background with output redirected: 'python migrate.py > migration.log 2>&1 &'. This frees the terminal. I use 'tail -f migration.log' to watch progress in real time and 'jobs' to check the background job status. (Result) Migration runs uninterrupted while I continue monitoring.

questions.question: Your team installs Docker on 10 EC2 instances and the output floods all the terminals. How do you silence it while keeping a log?
questions.answer: (Situation) Docker install output cluttering all terminals. (Task) Run silently with audit trail. (Action) I update the install command to redirect stdout and stderr to a log file: 'sudo yum install docker -y > /var/log/docker-install.log 2>&1 &'. This sends all output to a file and runs in the background. Each server gets its own log file. (Result) Terminals stay clean, full logs are preserved for troubleshooting.

questions.question: A developer needs to copy their application files from their Windows laptop to an EC2 instance. They have the PEM key. Walk them through the process using FileZilla.
questions.answer: (Situation) Windows developer needs GUI file transfer to EC2. (Task) Configure FileZilla for SFTP access. (Action) Open FileZilla, go to Edit > Settings > SFTP, add the .pem key file. Then go to File > Site Manager, create a New Site with Protocol: SFTP, Port: 22, Host: EC2 Public IP, User: ec2-user. Click Connect and accept the host key. Drag files from the left (local) panel to the right (EC2) panel. (Result) Files are securely transferred over SSH without needing the command line.

questions.question: You see 50 zombie processes in ps aux on a production EC2 server. What is the immediate impact and how do you resolve it?
questions.answer: (Situation) 50 zombie processes detected. (Task) Assess impact and resolve. (Action) First, I confirm that zombies consume no CPU or memory — they only hold PID slots. With 50, the immediate impact is minimal. I identify the parent process using ps aux and look at the PPID column. Killing the parent process causes init to adopt and clean up the zombies. For a recurring issue, I investigate the parent process code for missing wait() calls. (Result) Zombies cleared, root cause identified.

questions.question: A colleague asks why their background process with & is still printing to the terminal. How do you explain it and fix it?
questions.answer: (Situation) Background process flooding terminal despite using &. (Task) Explain and fix. (Action) I explain that & only detaches the process from the foreground — it doesn't detach stdout and stderr from the terminal. Linux doesn't auto-redirect output. The fix is to redirect: 'command > output.log 2>&1 &'. The '>' redirects stdout, '2>&1' also redirects stderr to the same file, and '&' runs it in background. (Result) Terminal stays clean, all output preserved in the log file.

questions.question: You need to connect to an EC2 instance via SFTP but FileZilla keeps saying 'Server refused our key'. Describe your troubleshooting steps.
questions.answer: (Situation) SFTP key rejection. (Task) Diagnose and fix connection. (Action) Step 1: Go to Edit > Settings > SFTP and check for duplicate key entries — remove all and re-add only the correct .pem file. Step 2: Verify the .pem file matches the key pair used to launch the EC2 instance. Step 3: Check EC2 Security Group has port 22 open. Step 4: Confirm the username is correct (ec2-user for Amazon Linux, ubuntu for Ubuntu). Step 5: Check the instance is in running state. (Result) Identified duplicate key conflict, removed duplicate, connection succeeded.

questions.question: You're asked to install git, nginx, and docker on a new EC2 instance without being present to confirm prompts. Write the commands.
questions.answer: (Situation) Unattended software installation on Amazon Linux EC2. (Task) Install three packages without manual prompts. (Action) Use the -y flag to auto-confirm all prompts: 'sudo yum install git -y', 'sudo yum install nginx -y', 'sudo yum install docker -y'. For automation, these can be chained in a user data script or run sequentially in a shell script. After installation, enable services: 'sudo systemctl enable nginx docker'. (Result) All packages installed and configured without manual intervention.

questions.question: How would you check if Docker is running on an EC2 instance and what does each status indicator mean?
questions.answer: (Situation) Need to verify Docker service health. (Task) Check current status. (Action) Run 'sudo systemctl status docker'. The output shows: a green dot with 'active (running)' means it is running. 'inactive (dead)' means it is not running. 'failed' means it crashed. 'enabled' in the bottom section means it will auto-start at boot. I also check 'Active' timestamp to see how long it has been running. (Result) Immediate visibility into Docker health and boot configuration.

questions.question: A team member accidentally killed a process using kill -9 that was writing to a database. What are the risks and what should they have done?
questions.answer: (Situation) Force kill on a database-writing process. (Task) Assess damage and establish correct procedure. (Action) Risks of kill -9: no cleanup, open database transactions not committed, transaction log not flushed, temporary files not removed — potential data corruption. The correct procedure is: first try 'kill PID' (SIGTERM, graceful) and wait for the process to self-terminate. Only if it doesn't respond after reasonable time, escalate to 'kill -9'. For databases, the right tool is the database's own shutdown command (e.g., 'mysqladmin shutdown'). (Result) Identified that kill -9 bypasses all cleanup — always use graceful termination first.

questions.question: Explain how process states work in Linux from a system design perspective. When would each state occur?
questions.answer: Linux manages process scheduling through a state machine. R (Running) — the process is on the CPU right now or waiting to be scheduled. S (Sleeping/Interruptible) — the process is waiting for an event (I/O, signal, timer) and can be woken up immediately — this is the normal idle state for most processes. D (Uninterruptible Sleep) — waiting for hardware; the kernel puts processes here when hardware must respond before anything else happens. T (Stopped) — intentionally paused via SIGTSTP (Ctrl+Z) or SIGSTOP. Z (Zombie) — exited but waiting for parent to call wait(). The Linux scheduler moves processes between R and S constantly, with D being a temporary hardware-wait state that should be short-lived.

questions.question: How does the Linux process model relate to AWS EC2 resource management and cost?
questions.answer: On EC2, understanding process states directly impacts cost. Processes in D state (waiting for disk) suggest EBS I/O bottlenecks — you may need to upgrade to provisioned IOPS. High count of R state processes on a CPU suggests undersized instance — scale up. S state processes sleeping are normal and expected (idle workers in a pool). Zombie accumulation suggests application bugs — could eventually crash the server. For cost: background processes (&) let you parallelize work, reducing the wall-clock time your instance runs, directly reducing the bill. Proper use of systemctl enable ensures services come back after a scheduled stop/start cycle, preventing manual intervention costs.

questions.question: Compare foreground/background process management with AWS-native alternatives like ECS, Lambda, and Step Functions.
questions.answer: Linux foreground/background: Simple, no infrastructure — run on one EC2 instance. No retry logic, no fault tolerance, process dies if EC2 reboots. Best for quick scripts and development. AWS ECS/Fargate: Containerized background processes with auto-restart, scaling, and health checks. Better than &. AWS Lambda: Event-driven short-lived background processing without managing EC2 at all — cost per invocation. AWS Step Functions: Orchestrated multi-step background workflows with visual monitoring, retries, and branching. The & operator is a Linux primitive — production workloads should use managed services for reliability, observability, and scaling. However, understanding & is essential for EC2-based automation scripts and bootstrapping.

questions.question: How does output redirection work in Linux and why is it essential for cloud automation?
questions.answer: Linux processes have three standard streams: stdin (input, fd 0), stdout (output, fd 1), stderr (errors, fd 2). By default all three connect to the terminal. Redirection operators: '>' redirects stdout to a file (overwrites), '>>' appends. '2>' redirects stderr. '2>&1' merges stderr into stdout. '/dev/null' discards completely. For cloud automation: EC2 user data scripts run as root with no terminal — output must be redirected to a file to be reviewable. CloudWatch agent captures log files — so 'command > /var/log/app.log' makes application logs visible in CloudWatch. CI/CD pipelines capture stdout — proper stream management is required for build logs.

questions.question: What is the relationship between systemd, systemctl, and init in modern Linux, and how does this apply to EC2?
questions.answer: Traditional Linux used 'init' (SysV init) — a sequential startup system. Modern Linux uses 'systemd' as PID 1, replacing init. systemd manages the entire system lifecycle: boot sequence, service dependencies, logging (journald), and cgroups. 'systemctl' is the client tool to communicate with systemd. On EC2: Amazon Linux 2 and AL2023 both use systemd. Services defined as systemd units (.service files) get managed persistence, restart policies (Restart=on-failure), and dependency ordering. This means 'systemctl enable' configures the systemd unit to be activated at the appropriate boot target. Compared to running background processes with &, systemd provides restartability, logging, and boot integration — which is why it is the production standard for services.
